meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.en: to happen, take place, go on
meanings.note: Что происходит? = What is going on?

examples.trans: What is going on? I don't understand.

examples.text: Мы не знаем, что с нашей дочерью происходит!
examples.trans: We don't know what is happening with our daughter!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'why'.

examples.trans: Why are we going so slowly?

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'to' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: There's someone here to see you.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

meanings.note: нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates

пускать.gloss: to let in, to allow to go

meanings.en: to let in, to allow to pass
meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to let in', forming an aspectual pair with 'пустить'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: The guard doesn't let anyone inside.

examples.text: Не пускайте его, пожалуйста! Это мой бывший парень.
examples.trans: Don't let him in, please! That's my ex-boyfriend.

meanings.note: person visiting a person, place, or institution

examples.trans: A visitor was sitting in the reception room.

examples.text: Это журнал посетителей мэрии из полицейских вещдоков.
examples.trans: This is the mayor's visitor log from police evidence.

examples.text: Зато в ресторане станет больше посетителей.
examples.trans: On the other hand, there will be more patrons in the restaurant.

пустить.gloss: to let go; to let in

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to let go', forming an aspectual pair with 'пускать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to let (in)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Пусти меня немедленно, мне нужно срочно поговорить с Викой!
examples.trans: Let me go immediately, I need to urgently talk to Vika!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'обчак').

examples.text: Мы не пустили Собчак с мамой.
examples.trans: We didn't let Sobchak and her mom in.

examples.text: Вчера вечером мы чуть не оставили Собчак без свободного столика.
examples.trans: Last night we almost left Sobchak without an available table.

examples.text: Говорят, сама Собчак написала отзыв о нашем новом меню.
examples.trans: They say Sobchak herself wrote a review of our new menu.

meanings.note: + instrumental; со before some consonant clusters: со всеми

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: мам! = casual 'Mum!' when calling her
Russian preposition meaning 'at' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('I have') (possession) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('from (ask from someone)') (просить у кого) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: short form: закрыт, закрыта, закрыто

examples.trans: I declare the court session closed.

meanings.note: Derived feminine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'party'.

examples.text: Лёля пойдёт с тобой на вечеринку.
examples.trans: Lyolya will go to the party with you.
We are having a party tonight.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('she') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Паша, я больше не хочу о ней слышать. Понял?
examples.trans: Pasha, I don't want to hear about her again. Understood?

поднять.gloss: to lift, to raise; to rouse

meanings.note: 'поднять людей' = to get people moving
'поднять людей' = to get people moving

examples.text: А я глаза на это закрывать не буду. Я подниму людей!
examples.trans: Well, I'm not going to close my eyes to this. I'll rally people!

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'stench', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Подожди, что это за страшная вонь?
examples.trans: Wait, what is this terrible stench?
She will raise a stink on the internet.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: International borrowing from English 'Internet' ('inter-' + 'network').

examples.trans: Look it up on the internet.
Look it up on the internet.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'price, cost' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Ого, двадцать тысяч рублей? Ничего себе цена!
examples.trans: Wow, twenty thousand rubles? What a price!

examples.text: Тогда цена выросла до семисот евро!
examples.trans: Then the price has risen to seven hundred euros!

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'can', forming an aspectual pair with 'смочь'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Этого не может быть. Это наша история.
examples.trans: That can't be. It's our history.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'strongly'.

examples.trans: The wind is blowing hard outside.

examples.text: Я так два года потеряла. Любила так сильно!
examples.trans: I lost two years like that. I loved him so much!

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'пасть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to fall', forming an aspectual pair with 'падать'.

examples.trans: The cup fell off the table.

examples.text: А потом на меня упал мусор с ветки.
examples.trans: And then rubbish fell on me from a branch.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('so') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('like that, so') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.en: after all, still, all the same
meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'ё-таки').

examples.text: Аркаш, мне москвичи звонят каждый день. Может, всё-таки передумаем?
examples.trans: Arkasha, the people from Moscow call me every day. Maybe we should reconsider after all?

meanings.note: accusative/genitive его (него after prepositions), dative ему (нему)
Secondary conversational sense ('it') (for masculine and neuter things) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'давать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to sell'.

examples.trans: How much are you selling them for?

examples.text: Конечно надо! Почём ты их продаёшь?
examples.trans: Of course I do! How much are you selling them for?
So you really are selling it?

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

meanings.en: to try, to attempt, to make an effort
meanings.note: Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to try, to attempt', paired with 'попытаться'.

examples.trans: He tried to explain the situation.

examples.text: Пыталась? С бутылкой вина в руке?
examples.trans: You tried? With a bottle of wine in your hand?

meanings.note: in the instrumental: 'кем ты работаешь?'

examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, who are your rivals?

meanings.note: short form 'нужен / нужна / нужно / нужны' + dative: 'мне нужна работа' = I need a job
Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'empty', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('empty-handed (of a person)') (colloquial) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Why did you even come here? Empty-handed!

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('your') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'idea' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Хорошая идея! Я сейчас же попробую.
examples.trans: Good idea! I will try right now.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'may'.
Secondary conversational sense ('it is possible') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Can I go and have a look?

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to go', forming an aspectual pair with 'пойти'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('expression') (to run for a second term) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'home'.

examples.text: А ты иди домой и делай уроки.
examples.trans: And you go home and do your homework.

examples.text: Так, мы идём к слепым. А ты иди домой и делай уроки.
examples.trans: Right, we're going to the blind people. And you go home and do your homework.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'готовка'). Common feminine noun meaning 'preparation' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Заготовка на завтра сама себя сделает?
Заготовка на завтра сама себя не сделает!
examples.trans: Tomorrow's prep will not do itself!

examples.text: Утром все повара начинают день с чистки и нарезки заготовок.
examples.trans: In the morning all the cooks start the day by cleaning and slicing prep ingredients.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'втра').

examples.text: Позвони мне вечером. Договоримся на завтра.
examples.trans: Call me this evening. We'll arrange something for tomorrow.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: А с Пашей я снова чувствую себя женщиной.
examples.trans: And with Pasha I feel like a woman again.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'делать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to do', forming an aspectual pair with 'делать'.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).
Secondary conversational sense ('cuisine, cooking') (русская кухня = Russian cuisine) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Three rooms and a big kitchen.
And the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'until' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('goodbye') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Declinable feminine noun meaning 'meeting', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('see you') (in 'до встречи' = until we meet) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Решается ваш вопрос, Клавдия Викторовна! Вы не видите, у меня встреча?
examples.trans: Your question is being sorted out, Klavdia Viktorovna! Can't you see I have a meeting?
